lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.name: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.headline: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes: what the NHS and UK charities list
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.summary: The NHS advises everyone with high blood pressure to make lifestyle changes, such as eating less salt, being more active and cutting back on alcohol.
keyPoints: The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes, with or without medicine.
The NHS gives a limit of no more than 6g of salt a day for adults, and much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods.
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day, partly because they contain potassium.
The NHS also lists regular activity, losing weight if overweight, keeping alcohol low and stopping smoking.

body.heading: Do lifestyle changes matter if medicine is offered?
body.body:
The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes. Whether medicine is needed as well depends on the blood pressure readings and on the person's risk of heart attack or stroke. NICE publishes a patient decision aid for adults, titled How do I control my blood pressure? Lifestyle options and choice of medicines.

The NHS lists the main changes as eating less salt, eating a healthy balanced diet, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, being more active, losing weight if overweight and stopping smoking.

body.heading: What do the sources say about salt?
body.body:
The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day. The NHS says much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods such as bread, breakfast cereal and ready meals. Blood Pressure UK says most people eat almost twice the recommended six grams a day.

The NHS salt page lists foods that are high in salt, such as bacon, cheese, stock cubes, soy sauce and salted nuts. When a label lists only sodium, multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. NICE recommends that clinicians encourage people to keep their dietary sodium intake low. Blood Pressure UK says salt substitutes made from potassium chloride can be high in potassium, so people with kidney problems or diabetes are advised to check with a doctor or nurse first.

body.heading: What about fruit, vegetables and potassium?
body.body:
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day. It says they also contain potassium, which can help to balance the effects of salt. Canned, frozen and dried fruit and vegetables also count, and the charity advises choosing canned products without added salt or sugar. The British Heart Foundation explains that potassium helps the kidneys remove sodium from the blood and pass it out in urine.

The British Heart Foundation describes the DASH diet as a plan that trims sodium while raising potassium, calcium and fibre. It contains plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy products, and is low in salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol. The British Heart Foundation advises getting potassium through food rather than supplements, as too much can be harmful.

body.heading: How do alcohol, weight and activity fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises against regularly drinking more than 14 units of alcohol a week, and says to spread drinking over three days or more. The NHS lists losing weight, if overweight, among the changes that can help lower blood pressure. The NHS advice is to be active regularly, with at least 150 minutes of exercise a week, and says moderate activity is enough.

body.heading: What else do the NHS pages mention?
body.body: The NHS also lists cutting back on caffeine and stopping smoking among the changes that can help. NHS dietitian fact sheets say supplements of calcium, magnesium or potassium are not recommended as a way to lower blood pressure. Sources do not all give the same figures, so the NHS pages are the ones used here for limits on salt and alcohol.

being-active-with-a-long-term-health-con.name: Getting active with a long-term condition
being-active-with-a-long-term-health-con.headline: Getting active with a long-term health condition: what UK guidance says
being-active-with-a-long-term-health-con.summary: UK guidance describes building up activity gradually from the current level, and the NHS suggests speaking to a GP first when there are medical concerns.
keyPoints: A GOV.UK resource says one in three adults in England live with a long-term condition, and that they are twice as likely to be among the least active.
The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines say health benefits also come from lower amounts and intensities of activity, particularly for people with low fitness and disabled adults.
The NHS says moderate activity is the level at which a person can still talk but not sing.
The NHS Better Health site has a We Are Undefeatable section for people managing a long-term condition.

body.heading: Why does activity matter with a long-term condition?
body.body: A GOV.UK resource, Health matters: physical activity, sets out the benefits of activity for preventing and managing long-term conditions in adults. It says one in three adults in England live with a long-term health condition, and that they are twice as likely to be among the least physically active. It is aimed at local authorities and healthcare professionals.

body.heading: What do the UK guidelines say?
body.body: The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines include advice for disabled adults. For disabled adults, the evidence review behind them describes 150 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a week, building up first in frequency and duration and later in intensity. They also describe two sets of challenging strength and balance exercises, twice a week. The guidelines say health benefits can also come from lower volumes, intensities and frequencies of activity, particularly for people with low levels of fitness and disabled adults.

body.heading: How is the right level of effort judged?
body.body: The NHS says one way to tell whether activity is at moderate intensity is that a person can still talk, but not sing. The NHS advises speaking to a GP first for anyone who has not exercised for some time or who has medical conditions or concerns, and making sure the activity and its intensity suit their fitness. NHS Tayside says that when activity is increased gradually the risk of serious adverse events is very low.

body.heading: Which symptoms need medical advice?
body.body: A Newcastle Hospitals leaflet lists feeling dizzy, fever or acute illness, and new sudden joint pain or swelling as reasons to stop exercising and monitor symptoms. The usual route in an emergency, such as severe chest pain or collapse, is to call 999. A Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust page says that if pain stops someone exercising, a GP might be able to recommend treatment or review medicines.

body.heading: What help is there to get started?
body.body: The NHS Better Health Get active page has a We Are Undefeatable section for people managing a long-term health condition. It suggests the Five in Five workout, a five-minute mini-workout designed for people living with long-term conditions, as a starting point. The same page points to the NHS Active 10 app for tracking walking and to Couch to 5K. In some areas a GP or physiotherapist can refer people to structured exercise programmes; one council scheme offers one-to-one sessions with a qualified exercise referral instructor.

eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.name: Eating well with type 2 diabetes
eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.headline: Eating well with type 2 diabetes: what Diabetes UK, NICE and the NHS say
eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.summary: Diabetes UK says there is no special diet only for type 2 diabetes, and NICE advises the same healthy balanced eating as for everyone.
keyPoints: Diabetes UK says there is no special diet exclusively for people with type 2 diabetes.
Diabetes UK says the total amount of carbohydrate eaten has the biggest effect on glucose levels after eating.
NICE sets an initial weight-loss goal of 5 to 10 per cent of body weight for adults with type 2 diabetes who are overweight.
NICE says nutrition advice should be individual and ongoing, from a healthcare professional with expertise in nutrition.

body.heading: Is there a special diet for type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says there is no such thing as a special diet exclusively for people with type 2 diabetes. Its advice is to choose healthier foods more often and to keep treats occasional. NICE tells clinicians to emphasise healthy balanced eating advice that applies to the general population when advising adults with type 2 diabetes. The NHS says changes to diet and activity can help control blood sugar.

Diabetes UK advises avoiding foods labelled 'diabetic' or 'suitable for diabetics'. NICE also discourages the use of foods marketed specifically for people with diabetes.

body.heading: How do carbohydrates affect blood glucose?
body.body: Diabetes UK says that even low-carb eating shouldn't be no-carb eating. It says the total amount of carbohydrate eaten has the biggest effect on glucose levels after eating. Its guidance favours higher-fibre wholegrain foods over refined carbohydrates such as white bread. NICE also says a limited amount of sucrose-containing food can replace other carbohydrate in the meal plan, provided total energy intake is not excessive.

body.heading: What about fruit, vegetables and protein?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says whole fruit is good for everyone, and that with diabetes it is no different. Diabetes UK's type 2 meal plan includes at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. Diabetes UK lists pulses such as kidney beans, chickpeas and lentils as protein sources, and suggests using beans and pulses to replace some or all of the meat in a dish. It recommends at least two portions of oily fish each week.

One NHS trust leaflet (North Bristol) describes, in its weight-loss section, a plate with half vegetables or salad, a quarter starchy carbohydrate foods, and a quarter meat, fish, cheese, eggs or pulses.

body.heading: Where do weight and activity come in?
body.body: For adults with type 2 diabetes who are overweight, NICE sets an initial body weight loss target of 5 to 10 per cent. NICE adds that smaller losses may still help and that larger losses over the longer term have an advantageous effect on metabolism. The NHS page on food and keeping active suggests at least two and a half hours of activity a week, with brisk walking, climbing stairs and more vigorous housework or gardening as examples. The same page describes a short-term low-calorie diet as linked to weight loss and lower blood sugar in some people, and says it is not safe or suitable for everyone with type 2 diabetes.

body.heading: Who gives personal advice?
body.body: NICE says people should get individual and ongoing nutrition advice from a healthcare professional with specific expertise in nutrition, adapted to their needs and culture. The NHS notes that people taking medicines that can cause hypos are advised not to miss meals.

diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.name: Looking after your feet with diabetes
diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.headline: Looking after your feet with diabetes: daily checks, footwear and the annual foot check
diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.summary: Diabetes can reduce feeling in the feet and slow healing, so UK sources describe daily checks and an annual foot check.
keyPoints: Diabetes can damage nerves in the feet, so they may not give a warning when something is wrong.
Diabetes UK advises looking at the feet each morning and again at bedtime.
A trained professional checks bare feet as part of the annual diabetes health check, which is free on the NHS.
Sources advise prompt contact with a GP, podiatrist or diabetic foot team about a hot, red or swollen foot or any new wound.

body.heading: Why do feet need extra care with diabetes?
body.body: Diabetes can damage the nerves in the feet, which reduces feeling; this is called neuropathy. Diabetes can also affect the circulation to the feet. Diabetes UK says that if feeling has been lost, a person may not notice an injury to the foot. Sources note that smoking reduces blood flow to the feet.

body.heading: What does a daily check involve?
body.body: Diabetes UK advises looking at the feet before putting socks on in the morning and again before bed. NHS sources describe looking at the tops, soles, heels and between the toes, using a mirror or asking someone for help if the feet cannot be seen. The signs listed include redness, swelling, blisters, cracks, broken skin and colour changes. NHS sources also describe washing the feet daily, drying them well between the toes, and moisturising dry skin. NHS sources describe moisturising dry skin but avoiding the gaps between the toes.

body.heading: What do shoes and socks have to do with it?
body.body: Diabetes UK says shoes and socks that are too tight, too loose or that rub can cause problems. It advises checking inside and outside footwear before putting it on. UK sources describe changing socks daily and choosing natural fibres such as cotton or wool, without holes or thick seams. NHS sources say people at high risk should not cut their own toenails unless a podiatrist advises it.

body.heading: What is the annual foot check?
body.body: Diabetes UK says a trained professional should check bare feet as part of the annual diabetes health check, and that the check is free on the NHS. The check looks at sensation and at blood flow in the feet. The result places a person in a low, moderate or high risk category for foot problems. Diabetes UK says that people at low risk may move to a check every other year, while those at moderate risk usually keep having yearly checks. NICE has a guideline on preventing and managing diabetic foot problems.

body.heading: When should foot changes be reported, and to whom?
body.body: Sources advise prompt contact with a GP, podiatrist or diabetic foot team about a hot, red, swollen foot, new damage to the skin, a change in foot shape, new pain, or a cut that is slow to heal. NHS sources describe seeking help the same day for signs of infection such as redness, swelling, oozing or a bad smell, and NHS Inform says to call NHS 111 for new foot problems with fever, shivering or feeling generally unwell. A foot that is changing colour or going very pale or blue, especially with new numbness or pain, is described as an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. When the GP practice or podiatrist is closed, the route is NHS 111.

sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.name: Sun safety and checking your skin
sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.headline: Sun safety and checking your skin: what the NHS and Cancer Research UK say
sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.summary: The NHS advises sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and 4-star UVA protection alongside shade and clothing, and describes changing moles as a reason to see a GP.
keyPoints: The NHS says sunscreen should show an SPF of at least 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection, and should not be the only protection.
Cancer Research UK advises seeking shade, especially between 11am and 3pm in the UK.
The NHS says sunbeds and lamps can be more dangerous than natural sunlight, and Cancer Research UK says any level of sunbed use increases skin cancer risk.
The NHS says a new mole, or a change in an existing mole, may be a sign of melanoma and is a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about sunscreen?
body.body: The NHS says the label should show an SPF of at least 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection. SPF measures protection against UVB, and the star rating, up to five stars on UK sunscreens, shows UVA protection; the higher the star rating, the better. The NHS says sunscreen should not be relied on alone, and that suitable clothing and time in the shade when the sun is hottest also matter. Cancer Research UK recommends SPF 30 or higher with a 4 or 5 star UVA rating, used together with shade and clothing.

body.heading: What about shade, clothing and cloud?
body.body: Cancer Research UK advises seeking shade, especially between 11am and 3pm in the UK. It recommends covering up with clothes, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses with UV protection. It says tightly woven fabrics are generally better than thin or loosely woven ones. It also says that more than 90 per cent of UV rays can pass through cloud.

body.heading: Are sunbeds a safer way to tan?
body.body: The NHS says sunbeds and lamps can be more dangerous than natural sunlight because they use a concentrated source of UV radiation. Cancer Research UK says sunbed use increases the risk of skin cancer whatever the skin tone, and that any level of use adds to the risk. It names fake tan from a bottle and spray tans as alternatives. It says up to 9 in 10 cases of melanoma skin cancer in the UK could be prevented by staying safe in the sun and avoiding sunbeds.

body.heading: How can skin be checked for changes?
body.body: The NHS says a new mole, or a change in an existing one, may be a sign of melanoma. It lists changes in size, shape or colour as the key signs, along with a mole that is swollen, sore, bleeding, itchy or crusty. Normal moles are usually round with smooth edges, whereas melanomas are often an uneven shape and may be more than one colour. Cancer Research UK and the Royal Marsden describe an ABCDE checklist covering asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolving change; sources give different size thresholds, so none is given here. Some melanomas do not arise from an existing mole; nodular melanoma can appear as a raised dark lump. A mirror or a helper can be used to look at hard-to-see areas.

body.heading: When should a skin change be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a mole that has changed in size, shape or colour, that is painful or itchy, or that is inflamed, bleeding or crusty. It also advises seeing a GP about a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks, including on the palms or soles. NHS 111 Wales also lists a dark area under a nail that was not caused by an injury. The route for a routine skin concern is a GP appointment.

preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.name: Preventing food poisoning at home: the 4 Cs
preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.headline: Preventing food poisoning at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and cross-contamination
preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.summary: NHS inform and the Food Standards Agency describe four steps for food safety at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination.
keyPoints: NHS inform describes four basic steps to food safety at home, known as the four Cs: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination.
The Food Standards Agency advises against washing raw meat, because washing can splash bacteria onto hands, utensils and worktops.
Cooked food is chilled promptly, and leftovers are reheated only once until steaming hot all the way through.
NHS pages advise people at higher risk of infection, such as pregnant women and people with a weakened immune system, to take extra care with some foods.

body.heading: What are the four Cs?
body.body: NHS inform describes four basic steps to food safety at home, known as the four Cs: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination. The Food Standards Agency also lists cleaning, cooking, chilling and cross-contamination as the four core areas of good hygiene. Food Standards Scotland promotes the four Cs as a way to avoid campylobacter food poisoning.

body.heading: How do hands and surfaces fit in?
body.body: The Food Standards Agency advises washing hands after handling raw meat, fish and poultry. NHS inform says hands, surfaces and equipment should be cleaned before, during and after cooking, and the Food Standards Agency says cloths and tea towels should be washed on a hot cycle and left to dry before they are used again. A Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust sheet advises washing fruit and vegetables before they are eaten. The Food Standards Agency says raw meat should not be washed, because water can splash bacteria onto hands, clothes, utensils and worktops. NHS inform gives the same advice about raw chicken: cooking it thoroughly kills germs, and rinsing risks spreading them.

body.heading: What does cooking food thoroughly mean?
body.body: NHS inform says food should be cooked through so that harmful bacteria are killed. NHS inform says poultry, pork and offal should not be eaten pink. Food Standards Agency consumer messaging stresses reheating leftover food only once, and making sure it is steaming hot all the way through.

body.heading: How do chilling and cross-contamination work?
body.body:
NHS inform advises cooling cooked food and putting it in the fridge within two hours. Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust says leftovers should be eaten within two days. The Food Standards Agency says pre-packed food can be frozen up to midnight on its use-by date.

NHS inform describes cross-contamination as bacteria spreading from raw food to cooked food, utensils or surfaces. NHS inform advises separate boards and utensils for raw and ready-to-eat foods, and a Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust sheet advises storing raw meat in a sealed container on the bottom shelf of the fridge. The Food Standards Agency advises using separate chopping boards and utensils for raw meat and other foods where possible.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk from some foods?
body.body: NHS pages on pregnancy and listeriosis list raw or runny eggs without the Lion stamp, pâté and ready-to-eat cold-smoked fish among the foods to take care with. The NHS says cold-smoked fish is safer if it is cooked until steaming hot.

looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.name: Looking after your teeth and gums
looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.headline: Looking after your teeth and gums: brushing, cleaning between teeth and dental check-ups
looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.summary: The NHS describes brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day, cleaning between the teeth and cutting down on sugary food and drink.
keyPoints: The NHS recommends brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day for about two minutes.
The NHS advises spitting after brushing rather than rinsing, because rinsing washes away fluoride left on the teeth.
Gum disease is driven by plaque; the early stage, gingivitis, can often be reversed with effective cleaning.
NICE says the interval between dental check-ups for adults should be no longer than 24 months and no shorter than 3 months for routine recall.

body.heading: How do brushing and fluoride help?
body.body: The NHS recommends brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day for about two minutes. It says electric and manual toothbrushes are both effective when every surface is cleaned. The NHS advises spitting out after brushing rather than rinsing, because rinsing washes away the fluoride still on the teeth. A fluoride mouthwash can help if it is used at a different time from brushing.

body.heading: What about cleaning between teeth and sugar?
body.body: The NHS describes cleaning between the teeth with floss or interdental brushes to remove plaque along the gum line. It says wooden toothpicks can damage the gums. The NHS advises cutting down on sugary food and drink, especially between meals. Its effect depends on how often the teeth are exposed to sugar as well as how much is eaten. Acidic drinks such as fruit juice and squash can also wear teeth.

body.heading: What is gum disease?
body.body: Bacteria in dental plaque build up on the teeth and along the gum line, and plaque is the main driver of gum disease. Gingivitis, the early stage, makes the gums swollen and red, and they can bleed. It can often be reversed with effective cleaning. Untreated, gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, which damages the bone and tissue that support the teeth and cannot be reversed, though treatment can control it. Gum disease is often painless, so it may not be noticed until a dental check. A Leeds Teaching Hospitals leaflet says smoking significantly increases the risk of gum disease, and the NHS lists stopping smoking among the advice for early-stage gum disease.

body.heading: How often are dental check-ups needed?
body.body: NICE guideline CG19 says the longest interval between oral health reviews for adults should be 24 months, and the shortest for routine recall should be 3 months. It says longer intervals suit people who have shown they can maintain good oral health and are not at risk of oral disease. NHS inform says people in Scotland are seen according to their oral health needs, which may mean more frequent visits or fewer if their oral health is good.

body.heading: Who gets free NHS dental care, and when is a dentist needed?
body.body: NHS dental treatment in England is free for some groups, including children under 18 (or under 19 in full-time education), pregnant women and women who had a baby in the past 12 months, and people on certain benefits. The NHS advises having red, swollen, sore or bleeding gums checked by a dentist. NHS pages say people not registered with a dentist can search for one on the NHS website, and that NHS 111 can put them in touch with an urgent dental service in England.

protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.name: Protecting your hearing from loud noise
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.headline: Protecting your hearing from loud noise: headphones, earplugs and warning signs
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.summary: The WHO and NHS sources say noise-related hearing loss is permanent but can be prevented, mainly by lowering volume, taking breaks and using ear protection.
keyPoints: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented through safe listening, although the damage is permanent.
NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume.
Reusable musicians' earplugs reduce the volume of music without muffling it, according to an NHS trust leaflet.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears.

body.heading: Can loud noise cause permanent hearing loss?
body.body: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented by following safe listening, although the damage itself is permanent. Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust says that once the cochlea has been damaged no treatment or surgery can undo it. The WHO estimates that 1.1 billion young people worldwide could be at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening practices. NHS inform says hearing loss often develops with age or is caused by repeated exposure to loud noise, and that it is possible to reduce the risk of noise-induced hearing loss.

body.heading: What do the sources say about headphones?
body.body: NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume. The Royal Free London leaflet says noise-cancelling headphones can help because they remove the urge to turn the volume up to drown out outside noise. The WHO advises keeping the volume low, taking short listening breaks and, where possible, using carefully fitted noise-cancelling earphones. The WHO's recommendations for young people include limiting daily use of personal audio devices to less than one hour. The Royal Free leaflet advises keeping the volume modest and taking a short break from headphones each hour. The WHO notes that smartphone apps can help monitor listening levels.

body.heading: How do earplugs and earmuffs differ?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe earplugs and earmuffs as working by reducing the level of sound that reaches the ears. Earplugs are described as probably best for long-term use, while very high noise levels may call for high-attenuation earmuffs. The Royal Free leaflet says reusable musicians' earplugs lower the volume of music without muffling it. Torbay and South Devon audiology says ordinary pharmacy earplugs are often designed for swimming or background noise and may not protect against damaging noise. The WHO recommends wearing earplugs in noisy venues.

body.heading: What are the warning signs of too much noise?
body.body: It suggests moving away from loudspeakers at loud events and taking a break from the noise every 15 minutes. RNID warns of a risk of hearing damage after just 15 minutes in a nightclub playing music at an average of 100 decibels without earplugs. The WHO advises watching for signs of hearing loss, such as ringing in the ears or trouble hearing some sounds or conversations.

body.heading: When does a change in hearing need medical advice?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears, hearing that has worsened over days or weeks, or hearing loss with earache or discharge from the ear. It advises a routine GP appointment when hearing is getting gradually worse. Arrangements for hearing assessments vary by area, and some NHS audiology services ask for a referral from a GP.

eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.name: Eye tests: who gets a free NHS sight test
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.headline: Eye tests: what happens and who is entitled to a free NHS sight test in England
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.summary: The NHS says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years, and lists who can have a free NHS sight test in England.
keyPoints: An optometrist checks vision and the health of the eyes, and can spot conditions such as glaucoma and cataracts.
The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly and is usually picked up at routine eye tests.
People aged 60 or over, people with diabetes or glaucoma, and under-16s are among those who qualify for a free NHS sight test in England.
The NHS lists sudden intense eye pain with a red eye, nausea and blurred vision as needing emergency care: call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What happens at an eye test?
body.body:
An optometrist or ophthalmic practitioner examines the inside and outside of the eyes. The aim is to check vision and eye health and to spot conditions such as glaucoma, macular degeneration and cataracts. An ophthalmic practitioner can prescribe glasses or contact lenses, and a dispensing optician fits them. If necessary, the optician refers the person to a GP or a hospital eye clinic for further tests.

When glaucoma is suspected, the NHS says the first checks are quick and painless and include vision tests and measurements of the pressure inside the eye. If glaucoma is suspected, referral to an eye specialist called an ophthalmologist follows for further tests.

body.heading: Why have tests when vision seems fine?
body.body: The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly over many years and is usually picked up during routine eye tests. It says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years. People at higher risk of glaucoma, for example those with a parent, brother or sister who has it, may be advised to have tests more often.

body.heading: Who can have a free NHS sight test in England?
body.body: The NHS lists people aged 60 or over, under-16s, and 16 to 18 year olds in full-time education among those who can have a free sight test. People registered as partially sighted or blind, and people diagnosed with diabetes or glaucoma, also qualify. The list also covers some people at risk of glaucoma, including some with a close relative who has been diagnosed; the age and other conditions are set out on the NHS page. The list also covers some people receiving certain benefits; the NHS page gives the details. Everyone else pays for a private test; the full list is on the NHS page. In Scotland the rules differ, and NHS inform says all NHS eye examinations are free for people who usually live in the UK.

body.heading: How often does the NHS pay for a test?
body.body: The standard entitlement is a test every 2 years. An earlier NHS test can be arranged if the optometrist considers it clinically necessary. A person who wants tests more often than the optometrist considers necessary pays for a private test. Optical vouchers, which help with the cost of glasses or contact lenses, have their own eligibility rules separate from free sight tests; the NHS page sets out who qualifies.

body.heading: Which eye symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS trust information advises seeing an optician or GP about vision worries that are not sudden. Glaucoma can sometimes come on suddenly, with intense eye pain, a red eye, rainbow-coloured circles around lights, blurred vision, nausea or vomiting, and a headache. The NHS says these symptoms need emergency care, and directs people to call 999 or go to A&E.

how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.name: How to read food labels: traffic lights
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.headline: How to read food labels: traffic light colours, per 100g figures and salt
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.summary: Red, amber and green traffic light labels show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt, and per 100g figures allow comparison.
keyPoints: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt.
Red means high, amber medium and green low; energy is not colour-coded.
The colours are mainly based on 100g or 100ml, which makes comparing similar products easier than portion figures do.
When a label lists sodium, multiplying by 2.5 gives the salt content, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What do the traffic light colours mean?
body.body: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt. Red means a high level of that nutrient, amber means medium and green means low. Guidance suggests choosing products with more green and amber and fewer red. Energy, shown in kilojoules and kilocalories, is not colour-coded.

body.heading: Should products be compared per 100g or per portion?
body.body: The colours are mainly based on the amount in 100g or 100ml of the food. Using the per 100g column makes it easier to compare the nutrient content of similar foods. Portion sizes are chosen by manufacturers and can differ, so per portion figures may not be comparable between products. A serving can be as small as one biscuit, so eating two means doubling the figures.

body.heading: What are reference intakes?
body.body: The percentages on front-of-pack labels are based on guidelines for how much of each nutrient and how much energy an average adult needs in a day. They show how much of that daily amount one portion supplies. Where a label has no colour coding, comparing the percentage of the reference intake in a portion is another way to compare foods.

body.heading: How is salt shown on a label?
body.body: Some labels give sodium rather than salt, and the NHS says multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. The NHS describes a food as high in salt when it has more than 1.5g of salt per 100g, and low when it has 0.3g or less per 100g. The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day.

body.heading: Are these labels compulsory?
body.body: Government guidance describes front-of-pack nutrition labelling in the UK as voluntary. The nutrition table on the back of the pack is mandatory. Labels therefore differ between products, and the per 100g figures are the common point of comparison.
